entries.title: Anthropic IPO raises record $81.3 billion on strong AI demand
entries.summary: The five-year-old artificial intelligence powerhouse priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, shrugging off growing concern about a possible AI bubble and volatility in tech stocks.
entries.content:
Anthropic IPO raises record $81.3 billion on strong AI demand

The artificial intelligence company Anthropic said on Wednesday it sold more than 956 million shares at a price of $83 a piece in a record-breaking initial public offering that makes it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

The five-year-old AI powerhouse raised around $79.4 billion through the offering, exceeding the $75 billion IPO haul of Elon Musk's SpaceX earlier this year. Anthropic said in a statement that "certain stockholders" also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO, bringing the total haul to more than $81.3 billion.

Anthropic's shares will start trading publicly on Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

The listing was oversubscribed, despite coming at a time of growing concern about a possible AI bubble and volatility in tech stocks.

The number of shares sold and the price exceeded Anthropic's original expectations. The listing prospectus targeted a sale of 825 million shares at $70 to $78 per share.

Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

entries.title: The law releasing the Epstein files passed one year ago. What do his victims say?
entries.summary: It's been a year since the House passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, forcing the Justice Department to release millions of files connected to the convicted sex offender. His victims speak out.
entries.content:
The law releasing the Epstein files passed one year ago. What do his victims say?

It's been a year since the House passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, forcing the Justice Department to release millions of files connected to the convicted sex offender. His victims speak out.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

Now we turn to an effort to shed light on the crimes of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, an effort that, in some cases, revictimized the women he abused. It's been a year since a new law required the Justice Department to release millions of files related to the Epstein investigation. But when the files were made public last year, so were the names and even phone numbers of some of the women he targeted. NPR's Ava Berger spoke with two Epstein survivors and to the sister-in-law of one survivor who died by suicide.

ANNIE FARMER: My name's Annie Farmer. I was 16 years old when I was abused by Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell.

DANI BENSKY: My name is Dani Bensky, and I was 17 years old when I met Jeffrey Epstein.

AMANDA ROBERTS: My name is Amanda Roberts, and I am a survivor of childhood sexual abuse, and I am the sister-in-law of Virginia Roberts Giuffre, one of the most prominent survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell.

FARMER: There has been so much that's happened in the last 12 months and, really, in the lead-up, you know, to the passing of the legislation, as well - was very busy and very chaotic.

BENSKY: I keep thinking about that day. We sat in the gallery of the House, and we got to watch the votes come in. And it was so surreal to sit there and just watch the board and watch everything start to flip to yes. We went from that moment, and, you know, tears were streaming as we passed this new law.

ROBERTS: There was this feeling of we knew the pain that each other carried. And there was this moment of unity, and it was that feeling, that unity, that courage, together, that drove this entire year.

FARMER: The moment of joy that comes to mind for me from this year was actually the day that the files were released. I think that there - as more people in the public have become aware of both the extent of the crimes and also the amount of information that was gathered by the government about those crimes, there has been a sense of validation.

BENSKY: But then I did find my name in a memo pad. It certainly wasn't redacted, as it had my phone number in it. And we started to see that the perpetrators were really being protected, and we couldn't find perpetrators' names and predators' names, but we could certainly find a lot of victims' and survivors' names. And so that felt really awful.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

BENSKY: There are a thousand girls, more than a thousand girls and women that have been abused in those files. And so, yeah, you might be talking about some powerful people, but you're also talking about over a thousand lives that have been completely derailed.

ROBERTS: There is such an appetite for justice in this community, in our country right now that I believe if we just keep this momentum pushing forward, we will see real accountability for all abusers out there. And we can really see a societal shift that says it doesn't matter what power and position and money you have, we are all to be held accountable to the same laws and rules.

FARMER: I certainly hope that there's a future where I never have to speak the names Epstein and Maxwell. I think many, many survivors in this case are interested in their lives moving on and not having to look so much in the rearview mirror about, you know, what's happened here.

ROBERTS: If Virginia was here to see this, I would tell her that I'm so proud (crying) and that I wish that you would have held on just a little bit longer to see this. But I understand why she felt like she couldn't, because she had been failed by every single system in her life.

PFEIFFER: Virginia Roberts Giuffre was one of Epstein's most outspoken accusers. She died by suicide last year. That was Dani Bensky, Annie Farmer and Amanda Roberts speaking with NPR's Ava Berger on the one-year anniversary of the passage of the Epstein Files Transparency Act.

And if you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

entries.title: Why the Nvidia scandal is a national security issue
entries.summary: The Nvidia scandal has spilled over into the Trump administration, which is now under intense scrutiny for how it allowed America's top AI chips to end up in China's hands.
entries.content:
Why the Nvidia scandal is a national security issue

The Nvidia scandal has spilled over into the Trump administration, which is now under intense scrutiny for how it allowed America's top AI chips to end up in China's hands.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

For more than two weeks now, the tech world has been consumed by the rolling crisis around Nvidia. The company's cofounder and CEO, Jensen Huang, was pushed out after news reports of extramarital affairs that includes an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of being a Chinese spy. The scandal has since spilled over into the Trump administration, and now it, too, is under intense scrutiny for how it allowed America's top AI chips to end up in China's hands. NPR's Ryan Lucas and Shannon Bond have been digging into this. Hey there.

SHANNON BOND, BYLINE: Hey there.

RYAN LUCAS, BYLINE: Hi, Scott.

DETROW: So the coverage so far has been about all the scandalous details of Huang's personal life, but this is a national security scandal. Tell us more about that.

LUCAS: Well, right. And China, of course, is a superpower. It has the economic and military might that puts it almost on equal footing with the United States, and China and the U.S., of course, are in a race to develop artificial intelligence. And AI has implications in all facets of life, including cybersecurity, on the military battlefield and technological development in the economy. So the trickle-down effects of this are enormous. And so protecting the current American technological lead in AI is seen is very much a national security issue.

BOND: And President Trump really sees this AI race with China as a binary win-lose situation. So here's how he described it back in September.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: We're leading China in AI. We're the most sophisticated country in the world. And frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins.

BOND: And look, Nvidia makes these chips that are really crucial to AI development. And so Jensen Huang has long argued that American companies should, in fact, sell these chips to China so that Chinese AI development is reliant on U.S. AI hardware. That view is not universally shared, including in the government, but it's one that Huang has really successfully pushed during this second Trump administration.

DETROW: And this gets to an important factor here - the way that Huang's views have shaped administration policies.

LUCAS: Well, look, the Biden administration took a hard line on this. It severely restricted the sale of the most advanced American AI chips to China to try to protect the U.S. national security and the country's technological edge in AI. Trump came into office in January of 2025, and things changed. Jensen Huang was actively lobbying the administration to loosen the restrictions. And for the past 18 months or so, America's most advanced AI chips, Nvidia chips, have been flying out the door to America's biggest rival, to China. I spoke to Chris McGuire about this. He worked on the national security council on AI and export controls. I asked him why China would want Nvidia's most advanced chips. Here's what he said.

CHRIS MCGUIRE: These chips are the lifeblood of AI. They're the most important thing that you need for AI systems and AI development, and they're also the single biggest differentiator between the U.S. and China.

LUCAS: Now, China can't make these top-end chips themselves, but despite the national security concerns, McGuire says over the last 18 months, some $60 billion in AI chips have gone to Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand legally. But those three countries can't support that level of AI buildout on their own. So some of those chips are suspected of having been smuggled into China. McGuire says the rest are in data centers that are primarily being used by China's top tech companies to train their own AI to make those models better. Here's McGuire again.

MCGUIRE: The reason that this happened is that the Trump administration did not enforce the license requirement that would have applied to those countries, and it's just enabled a massive technology transfer out the door.

LUCAS: Now, McGuire said this is potentially the biggest transfer of export control technology to an adversary in U.S. history, which, of course, begs the question of why and how that was allowed to happen. And there's an argument that Jensen Huang's personal relationship with Trump played a role here.

DETROW: So what exactly did that relationship - that relationship between Trump and Huang - look like?

BOND: Yeah. I mean, his profile was not this high at the beginning of Trump's second term. For example, he was not one of the tech CEOs who attended the inauguration, but Huang really successfully launched this campaign of personal diplomacy. And, Scott, as an example of just how close he became to President Trump, back in September, Huang was on stage at a big tech conference, and he took a call from Trump on his personal cellphone.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

JENSEN HUANG: Mr. President, oh, yes, sir. I got to tell you something. I - if it wasn't because of you calling, I would - I'm on stage.

BOND: He went on to put Trump on speakerphone and lavishly praised his leadership on AI. And you can really see how he's cultivated this relationship and has helped him become one of the most influential voices shaping the administration's AI policy. And Huang and others who share these views have framed making China dependent on American AI chips as a way for the U.S. to stay ahead in this AI race, which as I said, Trump really cares about.

DETROW: So what actions has the administration taken that have benefited Nvidia?

LUCAS: Well, the Trump administration has lifted restrictions on two specific Nvidia chips to allow them to be sold directly to China. The Trump administration also secured a massive deal to give the United Arab Emirates access to Nvidia's most advanced chips, a deal worth billions of dollars, and it did so despite concerns that those chips could end up, again, in China.

Now, at the same time, I'm told that there was a recommendation in the summer of 2025 to impose an export license requirement to send AI chips to Malaysia and Thailand over the concerns that we have been talking about, but the Commerce Department sat on that. It didn't move forward. And so those chip sales - the chips that are at the very heart of the current scandal - those chip sales continued. And only this week, in response to this rolling scandal that we've seen, did the Commerce Department move to restrict those chip sales and close that loophole.

DETROW: OK. So the Commerce Department made that move. Huang is out at Nvidia. What comes next?

BOND: Well, Huang and Nvidia's top lawyer are set to answer questions from lawmakers on Capitol Hill. That'll start after Thanksgiving. Those lawmakers are going to have a lot of questions, you know, about this relationship, certainly, with the suspected Chinese spy, but also about these allegations, you know, that there may be ways in which they were evading export controls.

Now, I should note, this week, Nvidia's board said it had formed a committee to oversee the company's national security policies and its compliance with export controls. You know, that's going to be a live issue. And, of course, Scott, Democrats are now going to be in control of Congress. So I think there is going to be more to come in terms of scrutiny and questions for Jensen Huang, but also for these administration officials and the decisions they made and what some of the thought process behind that and who might have been influencing that.

DETROW: Yeah. That is NPR's Shannon Bond and Ryan Lucas. Thanks to both of you.

LUCAS: Thank you.

BOND: Thanks, Scott

entries.title: Democrats nominate Jeffries for speaker, prep investigations into Trump's orbit
entries.summary: Democrats gave the official nod to Hakeem Jeffries to be the next speaker of the House. Meanwhile, Democrats are ramping up their plans to investigate the Trump administration come January.
entries.content:
Democrats nominate Jeffries for speaker, prep investigations into Trump's orbit

Democrats gave the official nod to Hakeem Jeffries to be the next speaker of the House. Meanwhile, Democrats are ramping up their plans to investigate the Trump administration come January.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

Democrats have been busy today on Capitol Hill. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is one step closer to becoming the next speaker of the House after a vote behind closed doors this morning.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

HAKEEM JEFFRIES: The people of this country are demanding bold, dramatic and transformational change. The status quo is unacceptable.

PFEIFFER: And Democrats are previewing their investigation agenda for when they take over in January. NPR congressional correspondent Barbara Sprunt is at the Capitol and is with us on the line. Hi, Barbara.

BARBARA SPRUNT, BYLINE: Hello.

PFEIFFER: So it certainly appears that Hakeem Jeffries is the presumptive next speaker. But was this a unanimous vote?

SPRUNT: It was not. There was some grumbling from newly elected progressive members who had said that they wanted to see new leadership. But Jeffries did run unopposed. This was an overwhelming vote of support for him. The vote was 251-11, and this sets him up for January, which is when the full House will vote for speaker.

PFEIFFER: And on the Senate side, things are not looking as clear cut. The current minority leader is Chuck Schumer. He's being challenged by Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen. What are their respective arguments for why they should get the top Senate job?

SPRUNT: Well, some Schumer allies have been using a sports metaphor when talking about this. Like, if the manager brings a team to the World Series, why would they then fire him? You know, a lot of people see Schumer as instrumental in flipping nine Senate seats for Democrats, far beyond what many in the party even considered in their wildest dreams going into this election cycle. But Van Hollen argues voters made it clear that they want change, and he says that that extends to Democratic leadership. Progressives seem very excited about him, but zooming out, it was moderates and centrist Democrats who really opened up the map in big ways for Democrats this election cycle, particularly in the South. So there is this tension - right? - between the why switch horses midstream and the other side that says, well, the moment calls for shake-ups.

PFEIFFER: And what's the general view on whether Van Hollen actually is a candidate who represents change?

SPRUNT: Well, perhaps unsurprisingly, it depends on who you ask. You know, he calls himself an underdog. He's positioned himself as embracing the populist economic policies that really resonated with so many voters this cycle. And fairly early on, he joined calls to restrict arms sales to the Israeli government, which has certainly endeared him to a lot of progressives. He's been increasingly critical of the Democratic Party and the way that congressional leaders have historically approached the Trump administration. But others point out he's not really a generational-change candidate. He's 67 years old, about eight-ish years younger than Schumer. He represents a blue state. He's been in politics for decades. And in fact, he's already chaired both the House and Senate campaign committees, so he's not a new face.

PFEIFFER: Barbara, in terms of the Democrats' agenda, since the election, they have been saying that they will aggressively conduct oversight of the Trump administration. Did they address that at all today?

SPRUNT: They did, indeed. Congressman Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on oversight and the expected next chairman of the committee, sent a dozen letters to President Trump's allies and some family members telling them to hold on to their documents for upcoming investigations.

PFEIFFER: Ah, sounds like a target list of sorts.

SPRUNT: Exactly.

PFEIFFER: Who's on that list?

SPRUNT: Well, the president's two sons, his son-in-law, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, her adviser Corey Lewandowski, Vice President JD Vance. Those are just a few. Democrats' targets fall into four buckets broadly - alleged corruption within the Trump family, corporate corruption, misconduct in the Department of Homeland Security and what Democrats call the White House Epstein cover-up. Now, the White House has rejected those accusations of misconduct before and has warned Garcia that investigations could constitute a crime. That is something that legal experts push back on.

PFEIFFER: Sounds like months and maybe years of coverage for you coming up.

SPRUNT: (Laughter).

PFEIFFER: That's NPR's Barbara Sprunt. Thank you.

SPRUNT: Thank you.

entries.title: After Nepal's epic flood, they're restoring their community ... and their lives
entries.summary: As the emergency response to the flood ends, aid workers turn to the hard work of rebuilding communities that lost everything. Many of those workers lost everything, too.
entries.content:
After Nepal's epic flood, they're restoring their community ... and their lives

"I thought I wouldn't survive," says Januka Dhital.

Just minutes before that terrible thought, Dhital was busy preparing snacks. She ran a catering service out of her house in Uttargaya, Nepal, and was getting ready for an event later that day. Her work was interrupted by a man on a scooter, warning of a flood. She stepped outside to look.

"When I turned around, I saw darkness, dust and what looked like the entire hillside coming down," she says.

She grabbed her young son and hopped onto the back of the man's scooter. They raced to higher ground, eventually reaching safety. But she didn't know if her husband and daughter were safe, since they were at work and school when the waters came.

"It felt unbelievable"

After hours of waiting and searching, they were all reunited. Her husband was naked, covered in blood and badly injured, she says, but alive.

"It felt unbelievable that our family had survived," says Dhital. But the wall of water and mud that descended from the mountains had obliterated their home, along with thousands of others. "We have lost everything. We have nothing now."

Dhital and her family are among the 100,000-some people whose lives have been upended by the devastating floods sparked by glacial melt, a phenomenon made worse by climate change. At least 1,500 have died, and more than 5,000 are still missing. Thousands are still living in temporary shelters or tents.

The flood damaged or destroyed seven health facilities, 23 schools, 10,000 toilets and 64 water systems, according to the United Nations. And there are early signs that malnutrition is spiking as winter approaches.

"The magnitude of devastation is unimaginable," says Shyam Pathak, a chief of health at UNICEF. The din of helicopters circling the wreckage looking for survivors has faded, he says. International attention and aid has fallen too, sources on the ground say, as the response turns to the arduous, but intimate work of helping these communities stitch their lives back together.

This disaster is somewhat unique, Pathak says, in that many of those doing the work are trying to rebuild their own lives at the same time. Dhital is one of them.

"I felt like I was losing my mind"

In the immediate aftermath of the flood, Dhital and her family moved into a holding center, one of a couple dozen that housed the displaced. They stayed there for about a month before moving into a relative's house. Those days were not easy.

"For almost a month, I felt like I was losing my mind," she says. "More than money, I am in great need of work."

She found that work through Helen Keller Intl, a nonprofit that's helping the response. After a short training program that included mental health support, she began helping her community rebuild. There's a lot to do.

"I go out into the community, we work with postpartum mothers, pregnant women and children under five," says Dhital. "This is the only thing keeping me going right now."

One of her jobs is screening for malnutrition among survivors.

Preliminary data suggest a notable increase. In Naukunda Gaunpalika, for instance, moderate acute malnutrition — a condition that can slow growth, weaken the immune system and become life threatening without treatment — appears to have gone up from 0.8% in June of this year to 8.7% in October, says Pooja Pandey Rana, who directs Hellen Keller's work in Nepal. These are likely conservative estimates too, she says.

"It's a big jump," says Pandey Rana, and likely driven by fallout from the flood.

In addition to losing homes, many families lost the gardens or local farms they relied on for nutritious food. "As a result, they have to depend on dried and packaged foods, such as instant noodles and biscuits," says Dhital. Poor sanitation and lack of clean drinking water is an issue too, she says. And many have lost their livelihoods, so they don't have money to pay for food.

Workers like Dhital are handing out supplies and cash to families in need. In some regions, that's a challenge.

Many of the communities along the flood's path were connected by bridges. More than 100 of them are now destroyed, according to the U.N. And for many living higher up the slopes, mountain roads were a lifeline that have now been severed.

"There still are places, especially in the upper north part of the impacted areas, which have been cut off by the flood," says Ayush Joshi, who works for the non-profit Save the Children in Nepal. "There is still a challenge to deliver food and life saving support to these areas."

"Our hearts cannot bear to see the destruction"

Pushmaya Tamang is a community aid worker trying to reach those areas. Often, she must cross the makeshift bridges hastily constructed to make up for the damage.

"The bridge shakes, making it difficult for elderly people to cross," she says. "It becomes dangerous when people try to cross the bridge from both directions at the same time. It almost overturns, making it extremely frightening."

Such damaged infrastructure is a start reminder of what's been lost, she says. Tamang is from a village in Nuwakot that's essentially gone after the floods.

"Our hearts cannot bear to see the destruction," she says. "The village that was once full of colorful lights and life has now become gloomy and dark."

Tamang's heart is heavy with grief over the loss of her younger sister, too. Many of the families she helps in her work with Helen Keller are also grieving unimaginable loss, she says.

"When we visit other affected families, we do not even know what to say or how to talk to them," she says. "We do not have the words to comfort or console them."

Many survivors need significant mental health support, says Pathak of UNICEF, which is teaming up with other aid organizations to mobilize health workers who can provide counseling. Like Dhital and Tamang, many of them are trying to help rebuild their communities while dealing with their own trauma.

"A hallmark of this response is that the health workers, despite being the victim themselves, are back to the work," says Pathak. "This has helped a lot."

"Everything has been wiped out"

Winter poses distinct challenges for survivors.

Colder temperatures are threatening those who still live in temporary shelters or flimsy tents. "Winter in these areas is very harsh," says Joshi. "Exposure to cold, overcrowded living, poor ventilation in the tent, damp bedding and inadequate clothing can also increase health risk."

Responders are winterizing tents and getting families into safer shelters, says Joshi, in addition to providing food and medical care.

In the longer term, there's the question of rebuilding what was leveled.

"We still haven't really seen [plans] on where to rebuild, how many homes are needed, how do we fix the water systems, how do you rebuild the schools?" says Pandey Rana of Helen Keller. "Like everything has been wiped out."

Preliminary estimates put the cost of rebuilding at roughly $5 billion, a steep figure for the small nation. The U.N. Climate Fund, aimed at helping countries harmed by climate change, approved $20 million for recovery. Domestic and international donors have contributed over $100 million in additional funds, but it's still far short of what's needed.

For now, aid organizations are focused on the immediate needs of survivors. Tamang says the daily work helps keep her going amid so much loss.

"What else can I do," she says. "Life goes on, and we have to accept what nature has brought upon us."

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

entries.title: Democratic Black women take over almost all state agencies in Georgia soon
entries.summary: In January, most of Georgia's state agencies will be headed by Black women who were all elected in the 2026 midterms.
entries.content:
Democratic Black women take over almost all state agencies in Georgia soon

Democratic Black women take over almost all state agencies in Georgia soon.

In January, most of Georgia's state agencies will be headed by Black women who were all elected in the 2026 midterms.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

Next year, Black women from the Democratic Party will be leading most government agencies in Georgia alongside the first ever Black woman elected governor anywhere in the U.S. DorMiya Vance with WABE reports on what the new leadership means for Black women.

DORMIYA VANCE, BYLINE: Georgia voters made it clear they wanted to see a change in who represents them next year.

MAUI BIGELOW: Every time there's a fire, y'all call Black women.

VANCE: Maui Bigelow (ph) cast her ballot in a south Atlanta suburb on Election Day. She said it was a pivotal moment to get more Black women into state government. That night, Democrats swept offices and celebrated historic wins. In Georgia, every state government office on the ballot went to Democrats. And Black women now hold eight of those 10 positions, including attorney general, secretary of state and, of course, governor.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

KEISHA LANCE BOTTOMS: Thank you, Georgia. I am honored to be your 84th governor.

VANCE: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta, beat Republican billionaire Rick Jackson, becoming the country's first-ever Black woman elected governor. She didn't emphasize her identity in her campaign. Still, voters were ready to give new candidates a chance, says Tammy Greer, a political scientist at Georgia State University.

TAMMY GREER: So the political environment happened. These women had the audacity to come forward. And they were able to get their message to translate across demographics.

VANCE: And when the state legislature convenes next year, Georgia will also have more Black women representatives. Greer says such prominence is new.

GREER: For so long, Black women have been in the background who have pushed others ahead of themselves while doing all the work.

VANCE: The governor is pretty powerful in Georgia. Bottoms can appoint and fill thousands of positions in state government. And she'll have a say over the state budget. Bottoms will have an ally leading the statehouse because Democrats won the majority there. Carolyn Hugley has been a state representative for over 30 years. She's nominated to become speaker of the House. She'd be Georgia's first Black woman in that role. She says this incoming class of Black women will be judged under a microscope.

CAROLYN HUGLEY: Sometimes people have unrealistic expectations of African American women in particular.

VANCE: She says she has dealt with prejudice and judgment throughout her career, including comments about her hairstyles and her clothes. And she expects harsh criticism ahead.

HUGLEY: That has always been a part of being a Black woman in America. And this is not new territory for me. I've been a Black woman for a long time.

VANCE: Hugley says, based on her experience, it's crucial that new leaders stay focused on their responsibilities as elected officials and not be distracted by any unreasonable backlash.

For NPR News, I'm DorMiya Vance in Atlanta.

(SOUNDBITE OF GLADYS KNIGHT AND THE PIPS SONG, "MIDNIGHT TRAIN TO GEORGIA")

entries.title: As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit
entries.summary: In a statement celebrating the historic drop in drug deaths, the White House pointed to successes since President Trump took office. In fact, the biggest progress happened under the Biden administration.
entries.content:
As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit

When the White House announced big improvements in the number of people dying from fatal drug overdoses earlier this week, officials pointed to hopeful new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showing U.S. drug deaths have plunged to their lowest level in roughly a decade, saving nearly 50,000 lives each year.

But leading drug policy researchers say the White House statement also made misleading claims about the timing and cause of the remarkable public health success when it said that gains occurred primarily over the last 18 months due to policies enacted under President Trump's leadership.

"The historic decline in drug overdose deaths demonstrates that America is unequivocally winning the fight against illicit drugs," White House Office of National Drug Control Policy director Sara Carter said in a statement.

Carter credited heightened border security under Trump and claims of success dismantling "narco-terrorist" organizations for the recovery. "Critically, this represents a an approximately 41.5% decrease in total drug overdose deaths compared to the peak under the previous administration," the statement said.

What the White House failed to disclose is that declines in overdose fatalities began much earlier, under the Biden administration, with most of the gains occurring before Trump returned to office.

"Since the spring of 2023, we have seen a steady decline in overdose deaths," said Vanda Felbab-Brown, a drug policy expert at the Brookings Institution. "The fact that it has been sustained is very important."

Fentanyl crisis on Biden's watch, then a pivot toward fewer deaths

According to CDC data, reductions in drug deaths began in 2023 and have continued steadily for at least 39 consecutive months — not 18 months as the ONDCP statement said. By the time Biden left office, fatal overdoses had already dropped by roughly one-third, an improvement described by addiction experts at the time as unprecedented.

Nabarun Dasgupta, a street drug researcher at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, was one of the first scientists to detect the stunning drop in overdose deaths. He said the trend toward fewer deaths began in some regions and among some demographic groups as early as 2021 and rapidly gained momentum nationwide.

"It was really the period early 2024 through spring 2025 where we were seeing the greatest rate of decline that we've ever seen," Dasgupta said.

Deaths from fentanyl smuggled into the U.S. from Mexico first began to rise in 2013 during President Obama's time in office and accelerated during Trump's first term. Fentanyl overdoses spiked sharply the first two years of Biden's presidency, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite progress, fentanyl remains the leading cause of drug deaths nationwide.

Dasgupta, Felbab-Brown and other and addiction experts credit the Biden administration for rolling out policy responses that included wider access to healthcare, making the opioid overdose medication naloxone more readily available, and negotiating a deal with China that disrupted the flow of industrial chemicals used to make fentanyl.

The Biden team also scored significant drug interdiction wins against the Mexican cartels that smuggle fentanyl. "We have certainly been seeing over many years, going back to the Biden administration, important efforts to crack down against them," said Felbab-Brown.

Dasgupta and Felbab-Brown both said improvements in reducing drug mortality have continued under Trump. They said it's important to have an accurate timeline of the overdose crisis because researchers are still trying to understand why deaths involving fentanyl surged and why so many fewer people are now dying.

White House on Biden role in declines

NPR asked the White House about progress in the fentanyl fight under Biden. In an emailed statement, ONDCP director Carter, a former podcaster, journalist and Fox News contributor, blamed Biden for failing to secure the U.S.-Mexico border and for allowing drug deaths to surge in the first place.

"While drug overdose deaths eventually began to decline following the peak, the Biden Administration doesn't get to take credit for overseeing the highest drug overdose numbers in history, then bringing them down from their own failure," Carter said.

Responding to CDC data showing drug deaths began to plummet much earlier than stated the White House announcement, Carter said "this could be misinterpreted as progress on a graph, but it was not progress."

According to Carter, the Trump administration is now well-positioned to build on overdose death reductions made over the last three years, in part by maintaining border security and by continuing to "relentlessly attack" drug gangs.

"We are dismantling and eliminating the violent cartels and drug trafficking organizations through coordinated operations," she said.

But Felbab-Brown at Brookings said she doesn't share the Trump administration's confidence that there has been significant progress "dismantling and eliminating" narco-terrorist organizations.

"I cannot think of one narco-terrorist organization that has been dismantled," she said. "They all continue operating and they are all very strong. They all continue smuggling drugs."

Military experts have also questioned the effectiveness, and legality, of Trump's ongoing strikes against civilian boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, described as smuggling vessels by the Pentagon.

Dasgupta, the addiction researcher at UNC, said he's also concerned about whether progress reducing drug deaths can be sustained next year as the Trump administration implements deep cuts to Medicaid passed by the Republican Congress.

The Congressional Budget Office has estimated the cuts could mean as many as 10 million Americans losing access to health insurance coverage.

"Medicaid is the largest funder of addiction services in the United States," Dasgupta said. "Cutting Medicaid eligibility or making it harder to access forms of effective addiction treatment is guaranteed to leave people out in the cold."

entries.title: Karl Kani dressed hip-hop royalty for decades. Now he's telling his own story
entries.summary: On NPR's Morning Edition, fashion designer Karl Kani talks about his new memoir, dressing some of hip-hop's biggest stars and why skinny jeans aren't for everyone.
entries.content:
Karl Kani dressed hip-hop royalty for decades. Now he's telling his own story

Hip-hop streetwear pioneer Karl Kani shares how he built his brand in new memoir

Fashion designer Karl Kani believes hip-hop needed its own clothing brand, one that reflected the music, culture and style of the artists who were changing fashion in the 1990s.

"Hip-hop needed the clothing brand that fit that look, who was from the culture," Kani told NPR's A Martínez on Morning Edition. "And I felt like the marriage between Kani and hip-hop was, like, heaven-sent."

Kani, born Carl Williams, started designing clothing in Brooklyn, New York, in the late 1980s. He was inspired by watching his father, a Haitian tailor, make matching linen suits to sell around the neighborhood.

At the time, hip-hop artists were already wearing names like Ralph Lauren, Tommy Hilfiger and Calvin Klein. But they weren't necessarily wearing the clothes as their designers intended. They favored oversized fits, mixed colors and created looks of their own.

Kani understood the appeal. He began making clothes as a self-taught designer in Brooklyn, New York, in the late 1980s. He helped turn that emerging streetwear style into a brand worn by some of hip-hop's biggest stars, including Tupac Shakur, Aaliyah and The Notorious B.I.G.

But the designer's ambitions extended beyond dressing famous musicians. He wanted to build an international fashion business that could last.

In his new memoir, Karl Kani: A Life By Design, Kani reflects on the creative instincts and business decisions that helped his brand survive long after the decade that made it famous.

Even his name reflects his ambitions. Kani, pronounced like "Can I?," came from the doubts he faced while building his business.

"Can I really come from the inner city and build a clothing brand?" he recalled asking himself. "I didn't know the answer to that question, but I knew if I call myself Kani, then every day I have to answer that question. Yes, I can."

After more than three decades in fashion, Kani also has some thoughts about what hasn't aged quite so gracefully: men in skinny jeans.

"I feel like a lot of guys kind of messed up when the skinny jeans phase came in," he said.

His advice? "Keep it simple, keep it slick and all black. You can never go wrong in all black."

In his conversation with NPR's A Martínez, Kani discusses his new memoir, the rise of his streetwear empire, hip-hop's influence on fashion and why skinny jeans aren't for everyone.

entries.title: Got a canceled flight? 7 clever ways to get rebooked fast
entries.summary: Flying somewhere for Thanksgiving or the holidays? Travel insiders explain what to do if your flight gets canceled or delayed — so you can quickly get to your destination.
entries.content:
A version of this story was originally published on June 17, 2025.

This year, nearly 6 million travelers are projected to take domestic flights for the Thanksgiving holiday, according to an AAA forecast published in November.

If you plan on being one of those travelers in the coming days, make sure you know what to do in case your flight suddenly gets delayed or canceled.

Life Kit

Listen to an audio version of this story here

Air travel has gotten notably worse over the past decade. In 2025, cancellations and delays surged, creating the worst on-time performance for airlines in the United States since 2014, according to a 2026 report by the U.S. PIRG Education Fund, a consumer advocacy group.

So, with holiday schlepping season kicking off this week, what's a weary traveler to do? Ahead, travel experts explain how to make rebooking flights less painful. Because what's worse than a canceled holiday flight is missing the holiday altogether.

Multitask! While standing in line, rebook your flight online

Most people react to a cancellation by heading straight to the nearest customer service desk and queuing up to rebook their flight. The problem with that approach? Everyone else on your flight is doing that too.

"You have 300 people getting off the plane. There's maybe one, two people trying to help everyone. That clearly is the least efficient way," says travel reporter Chris Dong. 

While standing in line, open up the airline app and rebook yourself, he says. There's often a seamless way to get it done, no customer service conversation necessary. During the holiday rush, when hundreds of other passengers may be trying to rebook at the same time, getting a head start on the airline's app can make an especially big difference.

See if an agent can help you at the airport lounge

If you have a travel credit card that gives you lounge access, head there to get one-on-one customer service. "Lounge agents are much more inclined to help you and are usually not as short-staffed," Dong says. "That can get you help quickly."

If you don't already have lounge access, see if you can purchase a day pass on-site. It may be well worth it depending on your flight cost and timeline.

Know what you're entitled to from the airline

All ticket holders are entitled to a refund if the airline cancels their flight and they don't accept whatever the airline is offering, such as a later flight and/or travel vouchers or vouchers for hotels or meals. However, most airlines in the U.S. aren't required to compensate you for delays or cancellations unless it's the airline's fault (think maintenance issues or staffing problems).

To find out what you're entitled to, check the Department of Transportation's Airline Cancellation and Delay Dashboard. Many major airlines have committed to giving passengers cost-free rebooking, meal vouchers, hotel accommodations, hotel transportation and more.

Once you know what your airline offers, say, a hotel, you can rest easy about what to do that night — and focus on rebooking for the next day.

Check what your travel insurance covers

Once you know what your airline will cover, check what your travel insurance will cover. Many credit cards include some travel insurance coverage, which can provide everything from trip cancellation to luggage insurance to any medical needs that might arise en route.

When rebooking, choose a flight earlier in the day

If you have flight time options when rebooking or flexibility in your travel schedule, choose the early-morning flight. They're your best bet to avoid delays or cancellations, Dong says.

If you're on the first flight out, there's little chance you'll have to wait for that aircraft coming in from another city because it's likely been sitting at the airport overnight.

This is especially worth considering during the holidays, when a single disruption can have a domino effect on subsequent flights. An early departure gives you more opportunities to get rebooked on another flight that same day if something goes wrong — because nobody wants to miss that family Thanksgiving dinner!

If you want refunds or flight credits, be nice to your customer service rep

If the airline significantly delayed, significantly changed (see DOT website for details) or cancelled the flight and you originally booked your ticket directly with your airline, getting your money back should be  no problem, even if the ticket is nonrefundable. But if you booked through a third party such as a travel agent or travel website, you'll have to go through them.

Remember that customer service representatives are likely dealing with hundreds of frustrated passengers during the holiday rush. Being patient and polite won't guarantee an exception, but it certainly won't hurt your chances, suggests Eulanda Osagiede, director of operations at Black Travel Alliance and chief operations officer at Black Travel Summit.

The best approach, she says, is to be "very nice, very friendly" with the customer service representative on the phone. So don't start yelling at them. Treating reps like the human beings they are can make all the difference.

Have a backup plan before you leave home

When you're traveling for Thanksgiving, Hanukkah or Christmas, a delay doesn't just mean missing a few hours of vacation. It could mean missing the big family gathering or a favorite kiddo's holiday performance.

So before you leave, take a few minutes to research alternative routes to your destination. Are there other airports nearby? Could you drive part of the way? Are there trains or buses that could get you there if your flight falls through?

It's also worth saving your airline's customer service number, downloading its app, and keeping your confirmation numbers somewhere accessible offline. If you're traveling with kids, pack enough snacks, medications, entertainment and other essentials to get through an unexpected overnight stay.

You can't plan for every possible disruption, but you can make sure you're not starting from scratch when one happens.

This story was edited by Malaka Gharib. The visual editor is CJ Riculan. We'd love to hear from you. Leave us a voicemail at 202-216-9823, or email us at LifeKit@npr.org.
